title: Self-Practice — Rutherford's Model Diagnostic Questions (Page 102)
notes: **Q1. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the nucleus of an atom contains the entire mass of the atom?** The fact that a minute fraction of alpha particles (about 1 in 20,000) were reflected back suffering a deflection of 180° shows that the nucleus must possess considerable mass — only a massive, dense centre could reflect alpha particles of considerable mass.

**Q2. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the central part (nucleus) of an atom is positively charged?** Some alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected by as much as 90° or even larger angles. Since alpha particles are positively charged, they could only be repelled by a positively charged centre — proving the nucleus is positively charged.

**Q3. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the atom consists mostly of hollow or empty space?** The vast majority of alpha particles (about 99%) passed straight through the gold foil completely undeflected, showing that most of the space inside the atom is empty.

**Q4. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the volume occupied by the nucleus is very small compared to the total volume of the atom?** Only a very small number of alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected through 90° or larger angles, indicating that the positively charged centre (nucleus of radius 10⁻¹³ cm) occupies a tiny volume compared to the whole atom (radius 10⁻⁸ cm).

**Q5. Why did Rutherford select gold foil for the α-particle scattering experiment?** Gold can be beaten into an extremely thin sheet (0.00006 cm thickness), thin enough for alpha particles to pass through and interact with individual atoms; gold is also a heavy element with a highly charged nucleus, producing measurable deflections.
